+# character, so the text can be cut there; pieces made only of \t-\r and

+_GPT4_CUT = r"\n(?=[!-~])"

+

+def _split_gpt4(text, compiled):
+    pieces = []
+    append = pieces.append
+    start = 0
+    for m in _stdlib_re.compile(_GPT4_CUT).finditer(text):
+        end = m.end()
+        append(text[start:end])

+    append(text[start:])

+    plain_findall = _stdlib_re.compile(_GPT4_PLAIN_PATTERN).findall
+    findall = compiled.findall
+    chunks = []
+    for is_plain, group in groupby(pieces, lambda p: plain(p) is not None):
+        chunks += (plain_findall if is_plain else findall)("".join(group))
+    return chunks

actions.reason: RegexTokenizer.encode_ordinary with the default GPT-4 split pattern now cuts the text at each "\n" followed by a printable non-space ASCII character. No chunk of that pattern can span such a point, so findall over the whole text gives the same result as findall over the consecutive pieces. Runs of pieces that contain only \t-\r and printable ASCII are split with the same pattern written for the stdlib re module. On those characters \p{L} is [A-Za-z], \p{N} is [0-9] and \s is [\t-\r ], and the possessive quantifiers can never backtrack there. All other runs still use the compiled regex pattern. The fast path is used only when the compiled pattern is the GPT-4 pattern with default flags. The stdlib re and itertools imports are local to the helper, so importing the module costs no more than before. Equivalence outputs are identical. encode_ir ratio is 0.9820, and the other metrics are within their limits.

journal.text:
I changed RegexTokenizer.encode_ordinary in minbpe/regex.py. With the default GPT-4 split pattern it now cuts the text at each "\n" followed by a printable non-space ASCII character. No chunk of that pattern can span such a point, so findall over the pieces matches findall over the whole text. Runs of pieces with only \t-\r and printable ASCII get a pattern written for that case.

Evaluation 1 was rejected. Equivalence held, but train_basic_ir worsened +9.43% and decode_ir worsened +4.89%, against a 1% limit. I reworked the edits. Evaluation 3 was accepted with identical outputs. encode_ir went from 628956573 to 617649506, ratio 0.9820. train_basic_ir was 1.0058, train_regex_ir 1.0043, decode_ir 1.0003, save_load_ir 1.0030.

The gain on encode_ir is small. The first version cost the other metrics more than it saved. The guard margins on train_basic_ir are thin.

I submitted 35 changed lines and the status is queued. Next, look at why the train metrics move at all when only encode_ordinary changed.
